text: 1. Laws of the Mitzvah etc. - [For reference, see] the Talmud - Yevamos 62, the Rambam - Laws of Marriage, Chapter 15, and the Shulchan Aruch Even HaEzer Seif (chapter) 1. The time of the mitzvah [i.e. when one is obligated] is from the age of 18, and one who proceeds [i.e. fulfills earlier than 18] is praiseworthy. [For reference] in regards to being involved in Torah studies [i.e. as potentially delaying one's fulfillment of the mitzvah] see in the aforementioned Rambam and the Maggid Mishnah [on the Rambam]. It is not necessary [to detail the laws regarding] the matter that is explicit in the Shulchan Aruch and Later Sages (Acharonim); however, there are some ideas and opinions to note with the help of Hashem.

How many children [does one have and become exempt] etc. - It is explained in the Gemara, Rambam, and Shulchan Aruch that it is necessary that there is to him a male and female [to fulfill the mitzvah, i.e. two children, one son and one daughter.] (Additionally,) there cannot be to him a sterile (saris) male nor an underdeveloped (ailonis) female because it necessary that (the children one fulfills the mitzvah with) be able to have children (themselves). If there is to him a Tumtum and a son or a daughter [that is one child of definite sex and one who is a Tumtom], we do not say [the following reasoning to say one fulfills the mitzvah]: (Firstly,) since a Tumtum is a safek [possibility] (that is possibly male or female, creating a potential fulfilment of the mitzvah with the other sibling who is of definite gender) as explained [regarding the Tumtum status as a safek/possible male possible female] in the Gemara here (Yevamos) 62a and the Rambam Laws of Marriage, Chapter 2 Law 25, and (secondly,) the Rambam's opinion, Laws of Forbidden Intercourse Chapter 18 Law 17 and Laws of Defilement of a Corpse Chapter 9 Law 12, that a possibility on a Torah (obligation or infraction) is treated leniently from a Torah perspective. [Ed. to illustrate regarding a negative command (Parenthetically it is a dispute if the Rambam says this regarding a positive command like in our case of procreation or just by a negative command which the cases cited discuss), the Rambam states in the Laws of Forbidden Intercourse (cited in the Minchas Chinuch) that if a girl is held captive, and the question was if she was defiled, which would disallow a marriage into the Kahuna (Priesthood). The Rambam states we are lenient regarding testimony, that is we accept testimony that usually would not suffice in other legal cases, because the whole issue is only Divrei Sofrim (i.e. an early Rabbinical enactment, which in this case is to be sure of a Torah infraction not just depend on a possibility that there is no issue) while from the letter of the Torah law, we would say since it is possible she was not defiled then she would be permitted.] If so, it is perhaps [to the Rambam] to him a male and female [despite one being a Tumtom], and he has fulfilled the command (per the reasoning mentioned, that 1) Tumtum is a Safek 2) Per the Rambam, a Safek is enough to fulfill one's obligation at least on a Torah level). This is not so [as stated]. Because a Tumtum is not able to have children, nor even to have intimacy because of (their genitalia) are blocked (or hidden). See Tosafos Yevamos 62a titled "From the Outside" that even when the balls appear from the outside, (therefore this Tumtum) is certainly male; nonetheless, it is not able to have intimacy at all, so the father (of this Tumtum plus in this case a definite female daughter or in any other case a Tumtum as stated above) has not fulfilled the command out of certainty, not just out of doubt.                                                            If one fathers an Androganus (Hermaphodite) and a son or a daughter, and an Androganus has to it both qualities of male and female [both genitalia etc.] as explained by the Rambam - Laws of Marriage Chapter 2 Law 24. [Ed. there are four stances of the Rishonim regarding the status of an Androganus - the Minchas Chinuch will analyze according to each if one of the children (of the two required) one has is an Androganus will one fulfill the mitzvah of procreation.] (Opinion 1.) The opinion of the Rambam is that in all matters the Androganus is treated as a safek (doubt), see Laws of Avodah Zarah Chapter 12 Law 4. Nonetheless, the opinion of the Rambam, Laws of Levirate Marriage Chapter 6 Law 2, is that an Androganus is not able to have children. This is also the opinion of the Rif there, end of Chapter 1. If so, there certainly one has not fulfilled the mitzvah because (the Androgynous child) is unable to have children. (Opinion 2.) Even to the opinion of the Ri (Tosafos) and the Rosh (in) Yevamos 82b and 83a in the sugya (discussion) thereof an Androganus that (the Gemara) decides legally (per these Rishonim) that an Androganus is a certain male [which is, of course, better vis-a-vis regarding legally fulfilling the mitzvah of procreation that requires a male and female than if the child was only doubtful male/doubtful female] nonetheless they are unable to have children (per this opinion) as explained in the Bais Yosef in the Tur, Even HaEzer Siman 172 Titled "And that which was written, However", and (the Bais Yosef) argues on the Tur that says the opinion of the Ri and Rosh is that an Androganus is a certain male, [meaning in a case of levirate marriage they would need to] do chalitzah or yibum, though (in fact) they would exempt from chalitzah or yibum [ed. the two ways to release the levirate bond that comes about if a married brother dies childless] because they are unable to have children [i.e. irregardless that they would be a brother because they are considered a certain male to this opinion]. See there (in the Bais Yosef). However (despite the Bais Yosef's explanation) from the words of Tosafos Yevamos 82b Titled "We Taught (in the Mishnah" it is clear that an Androganus is able to have children. [Ed. prior to discussing the ramifications of opinion 2  if one says that the Androganus is a certain male and can have children, he brings another source that discusses the issue prior as a matter of reference.] See the Noda B'Yehudah, Mahadura Tenina (first edition) Even HaEzer Siman 1 that deals with this distinction [if or if not per this opinion can the Androganus have children], and he brings the words of Tosafos; furthermore, see there what he brings from particular sefer [Chasdei Dovid, Bochorim Chapter 2, Titled "Androganus"] who dissects the matter. If so that (an Androganus) is able to have children, per this opinion that (an Androganus) is a certain male then legally he is like a complete son [and therefore in addition to a daughter would fulfill the mitzvah of his father]. And to the opinion that the Androganus is a safek (case of doubt) [Ed. Opinion 1] - if one also says they have children as these matters

"The laws of the mitzvah..." The laws of the Gid Hanashe [the sciatic nerve] are explained in the Shulchan Aruch [Code of Jewish Law], and it is not my method to expound on them, but with G-d's help I will bring remarks from other books or what HaShem Yitborach has favored me with, and I will write a bit about the laws of Gid Hanashe. We observe the laws of Gid Hanashe with domesticated animals and kosher wild animals, even among improperly slaughtered animals and sick animals which may not be eaten. If a domesticated or wild animals Kaf Hayerech [the protruding end of the thigh] is elongated instead of round this is difficult and not simple in the Talmud; shall we decide the question according to this particular animal and not prohibit its Gid, or according to its species and prohibit it? Likewise, what about a bird whose thigh is shaped like that of an animal? This is also difficult, and the solution in light of the doubt is that we prohibit it, but we do not punish someone (with lashes) for eating it, as is explained in Maimonides' Mishne Torah. Two nerves on the inner thigh are forbidden at a Torah level and one at the Rabbinic level, both on the right and on the left sides. We only observe the prohibition for kosher domestic and wild animals, but not non-kosher ones, which is like the opinion in the Gemarra of Rebbe Shimon who concludes from the part of the pasuk that reads "[the Children of Israel] do not eat...," those animals whose meat is permitted are subject to the prohibition of Gid HaNasheh, while those whose meat is prohibited are not subject to it. It is also said in the name of the RASHB'A that the Gid HaNashe is prohibited in human flesh because he follows the opinion that human flesh is permitted at a Torah level! This position is discussed in the Maggid Mishna [commentary on Maimonides], but according to Maimonides and others who say that human flesh is prohibited at a Torah level as a positive commandment, then the meat is prohibited and the Gid prohibition does not apply. Should you ask what difference does it make whether human flesh is prohibited by negative or positive commandment as long as it is prohibited at a Torah level, in my humble opinion and the book Sha'ar haMelech, Maimonides and many others think that nerves do not transmit flavor, therefore one must say that according to that opinion, one who eats only the Gid HaNashe from a non-kosher animal is totally exempt because he the pasuk in the Torah states that the Gid prohibition only applies to kosher animals and he is exempt from the prohibition of eating non-kosher animals because the gid does not transmit flavor (ie, it isn't really food). One who eats nerves and bones is exempt only from the Gid prohibition because even though these are not really food because the Torah prohibits it, but Maimonides writes that one who eats Gid HaNashe from an improperly slaughtered or sickly animal or of an Olah sacrifice (all of which is brought on the altar and not eaten) is liable twice, once for the Gid and once for the broader prohibition of eating prohibited food. Many are surprised in the name of the RASHB'A because if the Gid is not really food but a person is liable according to the language of the pasuk (which describes food that the Children of Israel "eat," ie kosher food), then he can he be liable for these? It appears these positions in the Gemarra and Maimonides conflict. Perhaps one is exempt for non-kosher species of animals but liable for improperly slaughtered ones. This will be discussed in other works and described later herein.

To count, etc.; the laws of the commandment are explained in the Rambam chapter seven of Temidin U'Musafin and in the Rif at the end of Pesachim, and these positions brought by the author you will find there in the Ran and the Ba'al HaMaor, and see Tosafot Menachot, and it is clarified in the Tur Orach Chaim and Beit Yosef section 489 and in the Shulchan Aruch and the later commentators, and see the Talmud Menachot "and you shall count for yourselves" that there shall be a counting for each and every one, and see Tosafot Menachot page 75b starting with "and you shall count" etc. regarding the Jubilee it is written "and you shall count" [in the singular] there the commandment is for the Court and it will be explained later with God's help in its place, and see in the Gemara and in the Magen Avraham there his opinion tends that one does not fulfill the obligation through the counting of his fellow even though he heard and it is not similar to Kiddush and the like where one fulfills through the hearing of his fellow for it is a Scriptural decree that each one is obligated to count for himself and see there that he brings in the name of the Beit Yosef that one fulfills if he hears from his fellow and see there that he left this law in a state of "Tzarich Iyun" (needing further study) and in the book Chok Yaakov his opinion is also that one does not fulfill through hearing from his fellow and in the Pri Chadash he debated and his opinion is that after the fact one fulfilled if he heard from his fellow and he brings in the name of the Sifri that the essence of what the Torah warned concerning a counting for each and every one was to exclude the logic that the commandment was only for the Court like in the Jubilee, and the later authorities have already elaborated on this, and see Magen Avraham that counting is in any language and not specifically in the Holy Tongue and if he does not understand the Holy Tongue and counted he did not fulfill, and behold the opinion of most of the early authorities is that counting in this time when there is no Omer is only Rabbinic but the opinion of the Rambam is that it is from the Torah see Ran Pesachim and Kesef Mishneh and Beit Yosef, and women and servants are exempt from this commandment for it is a positive time-bound commandment and see Magen Avraham wrote that nowadays they have made it an obligation upon themselves and this matter needs study and it is a new thing that women if they accepted upon themselves to perform a positive commandment from which they are exempt should become obligated because they made it an obligation upon themselves and I have not seen such in any place and it is not similar to the evening prayer see in the early authorities and here there are opinions that it is forbidden for them to perform positive time-bound commandments and according to all it is not a commandment at all and how shall they make it an obligation and I do not know the source of the words of the Magen Avraham, and what the author wrote at the end of the commandment "and it is practiced" etc. "and now in our great sins" etc. "we count the days and the weeks" it appears that there is a slight lack of language here and it seems that he holds like the opinion of the early authorities who hold counting in this time is Rabbinic and it should say "and now" etc. "even so we count the days and weeks" that is to exclude the opinion of the Rambam who wrote since we count the days and weeks it proves that counting is from the Torah and the author holds like most early authorities that counting is Rabbinic nevertheless we count the days and the weeks see in their words, nevertheless it is slightly difficult that he deviated from the opinion of the Rambam whom he mostly follows after at all events he should have brought the opinion of the Rambam and said that he holds like the logic of most early authorities as is his way in the whole composition, and behold it seems simple according to the positions of the early authorities who hold that if he did not count at night he should count in the day or if he skipped a whole day he should count afterward that he did not lose the commandment there is no difference between if he forgot or intentionally did not count or if he was not obligated to count such as a minor who became an adult during the days of counting or a servant who was liberated in the day nevertheless he is obligated to count for this is not of "completion" to say that if he was not obligated he does not need to complete like in tractate Chagigah regarding a lame person and several other places regarding prayer and Havdalah for this law of counting with all Israel is such that the commandment is that one day is not dependent on its fellow for if it were for the sake of completion he would need to complete and count also the count of yesterday and also if he forgot at night and counts in the day according to this position it is not completion rather the commandment continues and it is like one who went insane at the start of the night of Passover who is exempt from Matzah and afterward became sane in the night certainly he is obligated to eat Matzah for the whole night is the commandment and this is not completion so too here and this is simple, and according to the position of the early authorities who hold if he did not count one day he lost the count and the reason is as the author wrote that they are one commandment and since he did not count one day the calculation was canceled from him it seems also simply that there is no difference between if he did not count because he forgot or intentionally or that he did not count because he was a minor until the middle of the counting or was liberated since he did not count the calculation was canceled from him and this too is simple, but I am in doubt according to this position if the minor even though he is not obligated nevertheless counted in the way of minors or a servant counted before he was liberated also because he is permitted to perform a positive time-bound commandment as explained in many places in the Talmud and in the middle the minor became an adult and the servant was liberated if he is obligated from the Torah to count in his adulthood and his status as a free man in that year do we say that in obligation and exemption the matter depends and since he was exempt even though he counted nevertheless since it is one commandment and previously he was not obligated also now he is not obligated from the Torah and we do not compel him to count like all positive commandments in the Torah or perhaps since he counted even though he was in a state of exemption nevertheless the calculation was not canceled at any rate and he is obligated from here on and we find in the Mordechai regarding the Megillah he brought the logic of Rabbeinu Tuvia of Vienna brought also in Magen Avraham section 189 that one who is obligated Rabbinically fulfills the obligation for one who is from the Torah for one fulfills the sanctification of the day from the "Plag HaMincha" and above see there if so just as one fulfills the sanctification of the Sabbath in a Rabbinic time if so in a minor who became an adult since at any rate he reached the age of education previously certainly the time that he is obligated Rabbinically is effective to be obligated afterward from the Torah and the calculation is not canceled, but regarding a servant and he was liberated I am in doubt if he counted in his servitude if the calculation was canceled since he is not obligated or at any rate since he performed the commandment even in exemption it is effective for afterward that the calculation is not canceled and it needs study, and it seemed to bring a slight proof to this law from the chapter "He who comes upon his sister-in-law" [Yebamot] if he had children in his gentile state and converted since his seed is attributed to him he fulfilled the commandment of procreation even though the performance of the commandment was at a time when he was exempt for children of Noah are not commanded regarding procreation as explained in Sanhedrin nevertheless he fulfilled the commandment placed upon him at the time of obligation since at any rate he has children so too here even though now the obligation from the Torah falls upon him and previously he was exempt nevertheless the commandment that he performed in exemption counts for him now also that the calculation was not canceled and he is obligated from the Torah as it appears to my humble opinion, again I saw in the book Turei Even regarding Rosh Hashanah in that which is explained there "if they forced him and he ate Matzah" etc. if we say that a demon forced him etc. and surely we learned "sometimes healthy and sometimes insane" at the hour he is insane he is like an insane person for all matters and see there that he explained that is since he is like an insane person and an insane person is exempt from commandments the commandment he performed at the time of exemption does not exempt him afterward at the time of obligation since at the hour he performed the commandment he was exempt and the Turei Even asked from Yebamot regarding one who had children in his gentile state etc. he fulfilled procreation even though he performed the commandment at the time of exemption see there that he explained another explanation in the Talmud there and afterward he rejected the other explanation and his conclusion is like this logic and he settled it there from Yebamot see there, and according to him there is no difficulty at all for there is a great distinction between the subjects for certainly eating Matzah and Shofar and the like where the commandment is to eat Matzah and to hear Shofar if so certainly it is logical that the performance of the commandment does not exempt him if he performed at the time of exemption since previously he was not obligated at all and afterward he was obligated from the Torah that he should exempt himself with this but regarding procreation where the commandment is to have children and taking a wife and begetting is the preparation for the commandment for it is impossible to fulfill having children without this and the commandment has no interruption like other commandments rather all the days of his life is the commandment and in every moment he fulfills the commandment and this is the proof for Rabbi Yochanan himself holds there that if he had children and they died he did not fulfill the commandment we see even though he performed the commandment and begot nevertheless since they died the commandment was interrupted if so the essence of the commandment is that he has children therefore even though the preparation of the commandment was in his gentile state nevertheless now that he converted and is obligated in commandments and now he has children he fulfills the commandment because this commandment continues always and he performs the commandment in obligation only the preparation of the commandment he performed in exemption but in Matzah and the like in other commandments where the commandment does not continue rather the commandment is the performance if so after the performance of the commandment the commandment ceased certainly it is not effective what he performed the commandment at the time that he was exempt since now at the time the Torah obligated him he did not perform at all and what does it help what he performed at a time when the Torah did not obligate him at all but in procreation the commandment is not to perform rather only the preparation of the commandment but the essence of the commandment is what he has children and if they died he did not fulfill at all even though he took a wife and begot and the commandment continues if so he performs also now at the time of obligation the commandment therefore he fulfilled because he does not fulfill the commandment on account of his gentile state for also now in his conversion he fulfills like each and every one of Israel for the commandment is the children but in a commandment that depends on performance and now at the time of obligation he did not perform at all certainly he does not fulfill because he did not perform the commandment now and what he performed then he was not obligated at all and after the performance the commandment was interrupted and he is not performing and why should he fulfill with this the obligation of the commandment and see there in Yebamot that Rabbi Yochanan holds that in one who had children in his gentile state he fulfilled and he himself holds that if he had children and they died he did not fulfill the commandment if so since the commandment continues therefore he fulfilled even though he performed at the time of exemption because he fulfills also now at the time of obligation but that which depends on some performance and the commandment is interrupted certainly it is not effective what he performed at the time of exemption, and see there in Turei Even that his words are puzzling where he wrote that Rabbi Yochanan holds that he fulfilled that it is because of "for settlement" etc. even though Rabbi Yochanan disagrees with Rav Huna and holds that if he had children and they died he fulfilled procreation nevertheless here he admits etc. and in truth it is an oversight on the contrary Rabbi Yochanan holds if he had children they died he did not fulfill for "settlement" is required and see in the Talmud there and nevertheless here we can say that it is a continuous commandment even though it is one commandment nevertheless the name of the calculation was not canceled and he is obligated afterward in one who was liberated if he counted previously as it appears to my humble opinion with God's help, and similar to this logic you will find in the Ran chapter two of Beitzah regarding the distinction of the Eruv of cooked foods and between the Eruvs of boundaries and courtyards, and behold a servant is exempt for it is time-bound, and one who is half-servant and half-free man for those who hold that in counting one fulfills the obligation for his fellow if so he needs to hear from a completely free man to fulfill the obligation like Shofar and Megillah for one who is half-servant and half-free man even for himself he does not fulfill the obligation for his side of servitude cannot come and fulfill for his side of freedom and he needs to hear from another, but for the decisors who hold that one does not fulfill the obligation from another because "counting for each one" is required if so he is exempt from counting the Omer since he himself needs to count and his side of servitude does not fulfill for his side of freedom even though the side of freedom is obligated in all commandments nevertheless here what shall he do since the servitude prevents him and so it is written regarding Shofar if there is not another from whom he can hear he does not need to blow for himself for he does not fulfill at all and why should he blow and so in other commandments and it will be explained further with the help of God blessed be He, and it is possible to say that even regarding Shofar specifically if he can hear from another he does not fulfill through himself but if there is no other it is possible that he is obligated to perform the commandment himself because the part of the side of freedom is obligated and it needs study, and see what I wrote later in the commandment of Shofar, and a "Tumtum" (one of hidden gender) and "Androgynous" (hermaphrodite) their law is like in all commandments that the males are obligated and not women, and see Noda B'Yehuda second edition the law of an "Onan" (mourner before burial) on the night of counting his opinion is that he should count and there is room to debate his words, and if he forgot to count until twilight for those who hold counting in this time is from the Torah it is a doubt in a Torah law and one should be stringent and if counting in this time is Rabbinic it is a doubt in a Rabbinic law like Sukkah and Lulav see there chapter "Lulav and Willow," and regarding the matter of "commandments require intent" the law here is like in all commandments that depend on speech see in the Shulchan Aruch and this is not its place.

A person does not fulfill the commandment until the Torah is written in ‎accordance with the laws of a Sefer Torah. If there is a disqualification, even a missing or extra ‎letter, then a person does not fulfill this mitzvah, for it is not a Sefer Torah at all. The gemara ‎‎(Menachot 30a) asks, "Could a Torah be missing a letter? It is written(Devarim 31:26), 'Take this ‎Sefer Torah'!" The Rambam (Hilchot Tefillin, Mezuzahv'Sefer Torah 7:11) lists disqualifications and ‎says, "It does not have the status of a Sefer Torah, only as a chumash from which they teach ‎children." The Ran (Megilah) also writes that a person does not fulfill the mitzvah of writing a sefer ‎Torah with [a Torah that is] missing a letter. According to this, we cannot fulfill the mitzvah, for the ‎gemara (Kiddushin 30)explains that previous generations were expert in which letters to exclude ‎and which to include, but we are not expert. Therefore, we who are not expert might include a ‎letter in a word that should be written without it, or the reverse, and consequently we would not ‎fulfill the mitzvah [of writing a Torah] at all. The Shaagat Aryeh (36) has already suggested that we ‎might be exempt from this mitzvah today because we are not expert in missing and extra letters. ‎We can suggest that we are expert in the four chapters of the tefillin, for if this were not so, then ‎we could not fulfill the mitzvah of tefillin. We must say that since tefillin area constant mitzvah and ‎only include four‏ ‏paragraphs, we did not forget how to write‏ ‏it. As to the entire Torah, we are not ‎expert.‎‏ ‏Nonetheless, this remains difficult; writing a Torah is also a mitzvah, so how could people‏ ‏have failed to set their hearts against‏ ‏forgetting it?... How could the proper writing‏ ‏of the Torah ‎have been forgotten in the days‏ ‏of the Amoraim [recorders of the gemara]?‎‏ ‏In my humble ‎opinion, the explanation is‏ ‏that there are two types of missing or extra‏ ‏letters. One type involves a ‎missing or extra‏ ‏letter which changes the meaning of the‏ ‏word, or has the potential to change the‏ ‏meaning, like the examples cited in the‏ ‏gemara (Sanhedrin 4a)... According to theone who says ‎that we translate based on the‏ ‏word as it is written, a word which has an‏ ‏extra letter or is missing a ‎letter changes the‏ ‏message of G-d, for many laws will be‏ ‏altered from their true status. Even‏ ‏according to the opinion that we translate‏ ‏based on the word as it is pronounced, so‏ ‏that should ‎law does not change [based‏ ‏upon our incorrect writing], the Torah‏ ‏must still be written as it was ‎given. Therefore, when a Torah is missing a‏ ‏letter, since the Torah was given to us to‏ ‏be written ‎thus and not the way the word is pronounced [this change will disqualify ‎‏ ‏the Sefer Torah]… ‎However, other‏ ‏missing or extra letters do not change the‏ ‏meaning of the word…‎‏ ‏Certainly, the ‎first type of letters [i.e. the‏ ‏letters that would change the meaning of a word] were not forgotten… ‎but the‏ ‏missing or extra letters that would not‏ ‏change the meaning or cause harm by their absence ‎or inclusion were not‏ ‏known… and these letters, which do not‏ ‏change anything, do not harm this‏ ‏mitzvah and a person fulfills entirely the‏ ‏mitzvah to write a Torah with this act of writing… G-d ‎forbid that the Jewish‏ ‏people could not fulfill a biblical mitzvah‏ ‏for many generations.‎
Kometz Mincha: Mitzvah #237. And it seems to me that if one ends their own life with full knowledge and awareness of what they are doing, and someone else can save them, it's possible that they are not obligated in the prohibition of "don't stand idly by the blood of your neighbor" and for the positive commandment of "and you shall reserve [their property] to them" which comes to include returning one's "self" (lit. body) to them, for the obligation of returning a lost object does not apply in a case where someone loses their money intentionally / with negligence, as it's explained in Shulchan Arukh Choshen Mishpat 261. This prohibition is not cautioned against, as the Talmud challenges in Sanhedrin 73a: Why do we learn to rescue someone who is drowning in a river from "do not stand idly by?" Rather, we learn it from "you shall return it to him." This suggests that "you shall return it to him" includes returning one's body/life to them. One cansay the practical difference between these is with a case of someone who ends their life with full intention and awareness, that one is not obligated to "return their life to them," as they are not obligated to return their money to them. If so, you must say that the Torah wrote this prohibition of "don't stand idly by the blood of your neighbor," even though this too one is not obligated [in this case]. So it seems clear to me.
